papers.title: Learning about Markets from Models: Evidence from an AI Hiring Platform
papers.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used to not only inform, but make decisions. Sometimes platforms add value by pooling data across contexts to improve models' decision making---but when the optimal decision differs by context, pooling may not increase accuracy. We argue that a platform storing starkly distinct models across contexts nevertheless captures a model comparison externality. Together, these models reflect how decision makers respond differently to the same data in the current equilibrium. Policymakers can use this differentiation to prioritize interventions; firms can learn how they are already differentiated from competitors to focus future investments. Our evidence comes from an AI hiring platform used by large employers of low-skill workers. The platform uses a standardized psychometric assessment to create firm-specific models estimating each application's retention likelihood at that firm. Each firm's model is highly predictive for itself but no better than chance at other firms. We use these models to create a firm-application matrix: each firm scores each application, not only the ones it receives. An application's improved retention likelihood if submitted to a different firm is highly heterogeneous based on traits. Further, these gains are due to two distinct mechanisms. Finally, firms value traits differently even in this low skill market: they disagree about whether important traits improve or worsen retention at the margin. These insights are only possible when a platform can access both the full application pool and each firm-specific model. We explain the value of these insights to firms, policymakers, and platforms.
papers.topic_reason: Studies firm-specific ML models and market differentiation on an AI hiring platform.
papers.one_sentence: Analyzes firm-specific retention-prediction models on an AI hiring platform used by low-skill employers. Builds a firm-application matrix scoring each application against every firm's model, not only the firm it applied to. Finds models are predictive only within their own firm and firms disagree on how traits affect retention.
papers.screen_reason: Platform with firm-specific hiring models reveals market heterogeneity, externalities, and mechanism design insights from multi-agent behavior.

Firm-specific models built from a standardized psychometric assessment predict retention at their own firm but score no better than chance at other firms. Scoring every application against every firm produces a firm-application matrix, which shows heterogeneous retention gains from submitting an application to a different firm and disagreement across firms about whether important traits improve or worsen retention.

papers.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. A profile-generation LLM assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the learning data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

papers.title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
papers.abstract: We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $ε$-approximate Nash equilibria ($ε$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + ε$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $ε$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $ε$-NE, with matching instances for every $ε$. For small $ε$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $Θ(\sqrt{dε})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $Θ(hε)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $ε$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.
papers.topic_reason: Analyzes social cost changes from approximate equilibria in population-scale congestion games.
papers.one_sentence: Derives tight bounds on how social cost changes when players use approximate rather than exact Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games. Covers general degree-d polynomial latency games and single-commodity routing on series-parallel networks. Shows the possible relative reduction and increase scale as Θ(√(dε)) in general games versus Θ(hε) on series-parallel networks of depth h.

papers.title: Recommendations with Costly Verification
papers.abstract: A recommender faces consumers who can verify recommendations, but differ in their attention costs or in the salience of their choice of adoption. We characterize the conditions under which a technology that increases transparency by lowering the cost of verifying a product's quality will increase or decrease false recommendations. Without commitment, reducing verification costs never increases false recommendations, but when the recommender can commit to a policy, transparency can worsen both the quality of recommendations and consumer welfare. The necessary and sufficient condition is that the log-elasticity of the distribution of consumer cost types is decreasing. It can hold when the distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, or when it mixes sophisticated and naive consumers. Our results can be applied to platform-recommended listings, security ratings, and audits.
papers.topic_reason: Models platform recommendation transparency and consumer verification as a market design problem.
papers.one_sentence: Characterizes when lowering consumers' cost to verify a recommended product's quality increases or decreases false recommendations. Shows that without commitment, lower verification costs never increase false recommendations, but with commitment, transparency can worsen recommendation quality and consumer welfare. Identifies a log-elasticity condition on consumer cost-type distribution that determines the outcome.
